meta.accounting: Eight searches and ten successful external source reads. Local pinned reads are recorded in sources but excluded from the external fetch count. Failed Opik URL attempts produced no source.

entries.observation: Langfuse's overview describes the platform as open source, self-hostable, and extensible.
entries.possibleImplication: Treat the overview as evidence of a self-hosting posture and verify the exact platform license split separately.

entries.observation: The Langfuse observability section lists traces for LLM and non-LLM calls including retrieval, embedding, and API calls.
entries.possibleImplication: Its event model is a useful reference for a session evaluator that needs both model and ordinary tool or retrieval steps.

entries.observation: The Langfuse observability section supports multi-turn conversations as sessions.
entries.possibleImplication: Use a first-class session identifier above individual turns when ingesting coding-agent logs.

entries.observation: The Langfuse observability section supports representing agents as graphs.
entries.possibleImplication: A graph view can expose tool branches and retries that a flat transcript hides.

entries.observation: The Langfuse overview lists Python and JavaScript SDKs, more than 100 integrations, and OpenTelemetry capture.
entries.possibleImplication: Prefer an ingestion boundary that accepts native adapters and OTLP-like events instead of one harness format.

entries.observation: The Langfuse evaluation section lists scoring of live production traces.
entries.possibleImplication: A session-eval skill should support online scoring after ingestion as well as offline replay.

entries.observation: The Langfuse evaluation section lists LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.
entries.possibleImplication: Expose evaluator adapters with explicit model, prompt, and score provenance.

entries.observation: The Langfuse evaluation section lists code evaluators, user feedback, manual labels, and custom pipelines.
entries.possibleImplication: Support deterministic checks, human review, and custom evaluator hooks beside model judges.

entries.observation: The Langfuse evaluation section lists datasets and experiments for development testing.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow dataset snapshots and repeatable experiment runs for skill regression tracking.

entries.observation: The Langfuse overview lists a dashboard for evaluation results and links an Agent Skill, CLI, and MCP server.
entries.possibleImplication: A first-party skill can borrow the combination of human dashboard review and agent-readable query surfaces.

entries.observation: Installed Langfuse Python SDK package metadata for version 3.14.5 identifies the package as MIT licensed.
entries.possibleImplication: The SDK can be treated as an MIT-licensed integration component, while the platform license split remains a separate question.

entries.observation: The Opik repository comparison table labels Langfuse's core MIT licensed and its enterprise modules commercial.
entries.possibleImplication: Record Langfuse as MIT-core/open-core provisionally and retain a direct first-party license-page follow-up.

entries.observation: The LangWatch introduction calls LangWatch an open-source LLMOps platform.
entries.possibleImplication: Treat the product claim as an open-core platform claim and inspect the component split before reuse.

entries.observation: The LangWatch introduction says every LLM call, tool usage, and user interaction is tracked with traces, spans, and metadata.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a trace-span-metadata model that can preserve conversation context and tool activity.

entries.observation: The LangWatch LLM Ops card lists multi-turn agent testing against a simulated user.
entries.possibleImplication: Scenario-driven multi-turn tests are a useful complement to static transcript assertions.

entries.observation: The LangWatch LLM Ops card lists evaluations as experiments on datasets and monitors on production traffic.
entries.possibleImplication: Implement both pre-deploy dataset runs and production trend monitors.

entries.observation: The LangWatch coding-agents card names Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI, and opencode and describes sessions with cost per session, pull request, and team.
entries.possibleImplication: Per-session and per-PR aggregation is directly borrowable for Styrir skill trend reports.

entries.observation: The LangWatch Open Source section identifies an Apache 2.0 self-hostable core and a separate enterprise license under platform/app/ee.
entries.possibleImplication: Reuse only the Apache core surface unless the enterprise terms are separately reviewed.

entries.observation: The LangWatch introduction directs users to self-host with Docker or Helm.
entries.possibleImplication: Its deployment documentation is a useful reference for a local-first service option.

entries.observation: The Opik GitHub repository metadata reports Apache License 2.0.
entries.possibleImplication: Opik is the strongest permissive-license full-platform comparator in this bounded set.

entries.observation: The Opik README describes the full platform and backend as free to self-host.
entries.possibleImplication: A full local server can be evaluated without relying on a hosted-only control plane.

entries.observation: The Opik README lists full trace trees for multi-step agents and tool calls.
entries.possibleImplication: Preserve parent-child spans and tool boundaries when converting session logs.

entries.observation: The Opik README lists datasets, experiments, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics for hallucination, moderation, and RAG assessment.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a dataset-to-experiment flow with both quality and safety evaluators.

entries.observation: The Opik README lists production dashboards and online evaluation rules.
entries.possibleImplication: Trend reports should include production score and token-usage views, not only per-run output.

entries.observation: The Opik README lists a PyTest integration for evaluation in CI/CD.
entries.possibleImplication: Expose a command or test adapter that makes skill regressions fail in CI.

entries.observation: The Opik README documents Docker Compose through opik.sh and Kubernetes deployment through Helm.
entries.possibleImplication: Support a low-friction local profile plus a scalable deployment profile.

entries.observation: The Opik README provides an MCP setup for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, Codex, and opencode.
entries.possibleImplication: MCP is a practical agent-facing query and evaluation surface for session evidence.

entries.observation: The Opik README integration table lists Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenClaw tracing integrations.
entries.possibleImplication: Coding-harness adapters should be treated as first-class integrations rather than ad hoc import scripts.

entries.observation: The Opik comparison table labels Weave an open-source SDK or toolkit and says its self-managed platform requires a commercial license.
entries.possibleImplication: Separate an OSS client library from a self-hostable backend when classifying Weave.

entries.observation: The Opik comparison table labels Phoenix source-available under Elastic License 2.0 and not OSI-approved.
entries.possibleImplication: Do not equate Phoenix's open-source marketing with an OSI-approved permissive license.

entries.observation: The Opik comparison table labels Langfuse's core MIT licensed and its enterprise modules commercial.
entries.possibleImplication: Use the label as a comparison lead and retain a direct Langfuse license-page check.

entries.observation: The Promptfoo README says Promptfoo remains open source and MIT licensed.
entries.possibleImplication: Promptfoo is suitable as a permissive local evaluator or red-team dependency.

entries.observation: The Promptfoo README describes a CLI and library for evaluating and red-teaming LLM apps.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a declarative command-line harness for repeatable quality and security checks.

entries.observation: The Promptfoo README says LLM evaluations run 100 percent locally and prompts do not leave the machine.
entries.possibleImplication: A first-party skill should support credential-local evaluation for sensitive session transcripts.

entries.observation: The Promptfoo README quick start runs promptfoo view after promptfoo eval and labels the result a web viewer.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a local browser viewer for matrix-style evaluation results.

entries.observation: The Promptfoo README lists CI/CD automation and security vulnerability reports.
entries.possibleImplication: Expose machine-readable pass or fail output and a human-readable security report.

entries.observation: The Ragas GitHub repository metadata reports Apache License 2.0.
entries.possibleImplication: Ragas can be considered as a permissive evaluator dependency.

entries.observation: The Ragas README lists objective metrics using LLM-based and traditional metrics.
entries.possibleImplication: Use Ragas-style metric adapters for answer, retrieval, and structured task scoring.

entries.observation: The Ragas README lists automatic test dataset generation covering a wide range of scenarios.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow production-aligned case generation to grow a session regression corpus.

entries.observation: The Ragas README lists integrations with LLM frameworks and observability tools and a production-data feedback loop.
entries.possibleImplication: Keep evaluator output portable so it can be attached to traces from another observability UI.

entries.observation: The Ragas quickstart currently provides a RAG evaluation project template.
entries.possibleImplication: Ragas is best treated as a metric and dataset layer rather than a complete tracing UI.

entries.observation: The Ragas README lists agent_evals, benchmark_llm, prompt_evals, and workflow_eval templates under Coming Soon.
entries.possibleImplication: Do not claim a complete current coding-agent session harness from this README; keep agent support as an open proof gap.

entries.observation: The TruLens GitHub repository metadata reports MIT License.
entries.possibleImplication: TruLens is a permissive evaluator and instrumentation dependency candidate.

entries.observation: The TruLens README describes the project as open source and OpenTelemetry-native.
entries.possibleImplication: Use an OTLP-compatible normalized span model for portability.

entries.observation: The TruLens README says function calls, LLM generations, retrieval, and tool invocations are captured as structured OTEL spans.
entries.possibleImplication: Preserve ordinary function and tool spans rather than reducing a session to model messages.

entries.observation: The TruLens README lists latency, inputs, outputs, tokens, and cost recorded per step.
entries.possibleImplication: Use per-step resource fields for trend reports and cost-aware skill comparisons.

entries.observation: The TruLens README lists evaluators for logical consistency, execution efficiency, plan adherence, plan quality, tool selection, tool calling, and tool quality.
entries.possibleImplication: These evaluator dimensions map well to coding-agent behavior checks.

entries.observation: The TruLens README documents inline evaluation and offline batch evaluation.
entries.possibleImplication: Expose both live annotations and replayable historical session scoring.

entries.observation: The TruLens README documents an MCP span type that captures tool name, arguments, output, and latency.
entries.possibleImplication: Use MCP-specific fields when a coding agent delegates work through tools.

entries.observation: The TruLens README includes trace waterfall and leaderboard visualizations.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a waterfall for diagnosis and a leaderboard for cross-version comparison, while separately verifying HTML export.

entries.observation: Helicone's official open-source page identifies the project as Apache License 2.0.
entries.possibleImplication: The stated license is permissive for a separate integration or deployment reference.

entries.observation: Helicone's official open-source page lists ease of self-hosting and contribution as reasons for its open-source model.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow the explicit self-hosting and contribution framing, subject to feature-level deployment verification.

entries.observation: Helicone's official open-source page describes open source as a way to prevent vendor lock-in.
entries.possibleImplication: Prefer exportable local artifacts and documented APIs in the first-party skill.

entries.observation: The OpenLLMetry introduction calls OpenLLMetry an open source project for monitoring and debugging LLM applications.
entries.possibleImplication: Use the instrumentation layer without assuming that the Traceloop destination is open source.

entries.observation: The OpenLLMetry introduction describes non-intrusive tracing built on OpenTelemetry.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow standard span export instead of coupling the skill to one observability backend.

entries.observation: The OpenLLMetry introduction says traces can be exported to Traceloop or an existing observability stack.
entries.possibleImplication: Keep exporters replaceable and support a local file or OTLP destination.

entries.observation: The OpenLLMetry introduction supports supported LLM frameworks and direct foundation-model API interactions.
entries.possibleImplication: Provide both framework adapters and a low-level event capture path.

entries.observation: The OpenLLMetry introduction links Python, JavaScript, and Go setup plus annotations for workflows, tasks, agents, and tools.
entries.possibleImplication: Model agent sessions as nested workflow, task, agent, and tool events.

entries.observation: The W&B Weave GitHub repository metadata reports Apache License 2.0.
entries.possibleImplication: The public SDK or toolkit is permissively licensed, but platform deployment terms remain separate.

entries.observation: The Weave README describes logging and debugging language-model inputs, outputs, and traces.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a function-level trace API that can capture non-model transforms too.

entries.observation: The Weave README describes rigorous apples-to-apples evaluations for language-model use cases.
entries.possibleImplication: Use side-by-side dataset comparisons to make skill-version tradeoffs visible.

entries.observation: The Weave README says it organizes information across the LLM workflow from experimentation to evaluations to production.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a single lineage view spanning session capture, evaluation runs, and longitudinal reports.

entries.observation: The Weave README lists a Weights and Biases account as a prerequisite and notes a free tier.
entries.possibleImplication: Do not assume the SDK README establishes a self-hostable backend or an offline-only workflow.

entries.observation: The Weave README uses a weave.op decorator to generate a trace tree for decorated functions.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a low-friction decorator or wrapper for instrumenting arbitrary skill steps.

entries.observation: The Evidently GitHub repository metadata reports Apache License 2.0.
entries.possibleImplication: Evidently is a permissive report and monitoring dependency candidate.

entries.observation: The Evidently README describes an open-source Python library to evaluate, test, and monitor ML and LLM systems.
entries.possibleImplication: Use Evidently as a report and gate layer around normalized session metrics.

entries.observation: The Evidently README lists more than 100 built-in metrics from data drift detection to LLM judges.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a metric catalog and make each evaluator's version and threshold explicit.

entries.observation: The Evidently README says Reports can be viewed interactively and exported as JSON, Python dictionaries, or HTML.
entries.possibleImplication: Use portable HTML as the durable artifact and JSON as the machine-readable companion.

entries.observation: The Evidently README describes Test Suites with pass or fail conditions for regression testing and CI/CD.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow thresholded checks that can gate a skill release without requiring a dashboard.

entries.observation: The Evidently README says the monitoring UI service can be self-hosted in the open-source version.
entries.possibleImplication: Evidently provides a practical reference for a lightweight local trend dashboard.

entries.observation: The Evidently README lists dataset and user management, alerting, and no-code evaluations as Evidently Cloud extras.
entries.possibleImplication: Keep the OSS report surface distinct from cloud-only collaboration features.

entries.observation: The fetched Evidently repository listing includes examples/agentic_systems_tracing.ipynb.
entries.possibleImplication: Agent tracing has a repository example, but exact session schema and production support need a direct example read.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix README describes Arize Phoenix as Arize's open-source AI observability platform.
entries.possibleImplication: Retain the product's own label in the report but classify legal reuse from the fetched license text.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix LICENSE begins with Elastic License 2.0 and grants use, copying, distribution, and derivative-work rights subject to limitations.
entries.possibleImplication: Phoenix is not a permissive OSI-style dependency for a competing hosted service.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix LICENSE prohibits providing the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service with access to a substantial feature set.
entries.possibleImplication: Do not vendor Phoenix as a hosted Styrir product; use it only as a separately deployed reference or integration target after review.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix README lists OpenTelemetry-based tracing for LLM application runtime.
entries.possibleImplication: OpenTelemetry and OpenInference are strong candidates for the normalized trace boundary.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix README lists response and retrieval evaluation, versioned datasets, and experiments for prompts, models, and retrieval.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a trace-to-dataset-to-experiment loop for skill regression analysis.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix README documents local, containerized, and cloud deployment and a phoenix serve command.
entries.possibleImplication: A local server command is a useful operational pattern for reproducible report generation.

entries.observation: The pinned Phoenix README lists a CLI, agent skills, and a remote MCP server for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents.
entries.possibleImplication: Borrow a queryable agent surface rather than requiring humans to inspect every trace manually.

entries.observation: The local Phoenix Ragas integration guide evaluates an agent with tool-call accuracy and agent-goal accuracy metrics.
entries.possibleImplication: Ragas metrics can complement trace-native evaluation when a session adapter supplies the expected conversation shape.

entries.observation: The local Phoenix Langfuse comparison page claims that Langfuse places Prompt Playground and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations behind a paywall.
entries.possibleImplication: This conflicts with the current Langfuse overview's listed evaluation surface and must remain an unresolved versioned vendor-positioning contradiction.

entries.observation: The local Phoenix Langfuse comparison page claims Langfuse self-hosting requires ClickHouse, Redis, and S3-compatible storage.
entries.possibleImplication: Compare deployment complexity only after pinning both products and versions; the page has no publication or version marker.

entries.observation: The local Phoenix Langfuse comparison page claims Langfuse relies on outside instrumentation libraries while Phoenix maintains OpenInference instrumentation.
entries.possibleImplication: The current Langfuse page's OpenTelemetry wording and the Phoenix comparison should be checked against current integration docs before choosing an adapter strategy.
